item.title: Did I rejoin Ambitious Impact at the wrong time?
item.description:
Published on October 15, 2026 1:22 PM GMT

TL;DR: No, but you might, if you leave it too late: We’re hiring for seven roles, and the people who join now will shape what a much bigger AIM becomes. The first step is cheap -- an expression of interest form.

My worry

I rejoined[1] AIM in February. The team/culture and growth plans are more exciting to me than ever, but when I look at trends outside of AIM, in particular in AI capabilities, I’d be lying if I hadn’t asked myself if I came back at the wrong time..

The worry goes something like this: A new charity takes about five years to reach its peak scale, and some kinds of benefits (e.g. from education, or some policy changes) can take a decade to materialize[2]. If AI transforms the world before then[3], the majority of the new charity’s impact will go unrealized. So is starting new charities the best thing you can be doing with your career right now?

I grappled with this myself for months. I tried to put aside the sunk cost fallacy and consider whether I should be doing something else. My answer is that there's nowhere else I'd rather be right now. I hope you’ll come join me. This post will explain why.

Broad timelines imply a portfolio of bets, and AIM is an important bet within it

No one knows with certainty when (or whether) AI will transform the world.

  • Maybe the business side fails: the AI industry is super leveraged, so if it doesn’t sustain an unprecedented growth rate and if new investors aren’t convinced, the house of cards could collapse.
  • Maybe public pressure and political intervention slows progress (which could in turn bring the financial house of cards down).
  • Maybe AI will only gain the capabilities to transform the economy by learning from real-world experience, which requires diffusion that could take many years.
  • Maybe unknown-unknowns..

So instead of thinking in terms of short or long timelines, we should think in terms of broad timelines – a probability distribution. Even if your modal timeline is short, you should want the world to be making a portfolio of bets that maximise impact in expectation across that probability distribution. That includes bets that pay off most on longer timelines.

Your own career is one bet in that portfolio, and you should consider your comparative advantage when you make it. To choose an obvious example, if you have a track record scaling health programs in low-income countries (unusually rare and valuable experience) maybe don’t pivot to AI safety? But less dominating advantages, like having spent years steeped in a given cause (through work, study or volunteering) should factor into your bet too[4]. And experience isn’t the only kind of comparative advantage: plenty of roles, like marketing and comms (IMO), are more a matter of aptitude than experience.

[I recognize there are plenty who won’t find this persuasive, because they think the probability distribution is such that basically everyone should be doing short-timelines work. This post isn’t for you (but check out a comment I’ve left, which specifically IS for you). This post is for people whose timelines are consistent with people doing work that has impact over more than just a few years, and who have been waiting for someone to tell them it’s okay to be the ones doing that work. It IS okay! 🌈]

AIM is an important bet to have in our portfolio. I’m sure you’re sick of hearing about it by now, but a bunch of increased funding is already committed to highly impactful charities, with even more expected. We have a great opportunity and responsibility to deploy it as effectively as possible. If we get this right, we could make unprecedented progress on the world’s biggest problems, even eradicating some of them like humanity did with smallpox. But there are limits to how many programs existing organizations can run, and how far they can scale the ones they have. So we need a pipeline of ambitious new organizations to fill the gap.

Building that pipeline is what AIM does, and we've gotten pretty good at it (although we still have a lot more room for improvement). We've been refining our approach since 2018, having launched 69 charities, with 13 of the 16 that are old enough and in scope having been funded by GiveWell, 10 receiving funding from Animal Charity Evaluators, and several becoming pioneers in their fields, like LEEP in lead exposure and Shrimp Welfare Project in shrimp welfare.

Joining now means helping shape what AIM becomes.

Our plans are more ambitious than ever: We want to launch more charities, and better ones. Much like venture capital, charity incubation is hits-based: most of our charities are great, but a small number become field leaders so impactful that they account for the majority of our impact. To scale our impact, we want more of those field leaders.

The plan:

  • First, we’ll increase the chance that any given charity becomes one, through initiatives to improve the quality of our incubation (getting more ambitious charities up and running, faster) and to give our existing charities more support to scale up and reach their potential.
  • Then we’ll increase the number of bets we make by launching more charities.

We’re asking ourselves: what would it take to triple the number of charities we launch each year, and raise our hit rate at the same time?

We have the funding. We've just raised (pending due diligence) $21.5M for the next 3-4 years For context, our entire budget for 2026 is about $3M. So the world needs new charities now more than ever, and the money for us to incubate them is there. The hard part is doing three things at once: launching far more charities each year (see the chart below), raising their quality, and investing significantly more in supporting the charities we’ve already launched. That’s daunting, but doable with the right team 🤝

Our impact hinges on this hiring round. Talent is heavy-tailed: the gap between the best and second-best applicant for a job is often big. And because we’re about to grow fast, the people who join now will shape the processes, research methods and support programs that a bigger AIM will run on. So if you end up being our best applicant (and I’m certain that you are!), you can make a big difference to AIM’s trajectory.

And then there’s the people and culture

I can be a bit of an impact-maximising robot. And yet one of the biggest reasons that there’s nowhere else I’d rather be is that at AIM, I can bring my whole self to work, and I trust and feel cared for by my colleagues.

Of course there is an impact case one can make for this: I care a lot about helping beneficiaries, but from moment to moment at work, I’m not tapping into all the suffering in the world for motivation (and I think that’s healthy). Mostly, what motivates me is wanting to do right by my team. That motivation is a lot stronger when your team is a bunch of fucking excellent humans that you care deeply about. Stronger motivation makes for better work (<-- insights like this are why they pay me the big bucks).

But let's be real: the main reason I care about having great people and culture is that it makes AIM a great place to work. When I moved from earning to give to working at a charity, I suspected that working alongside value-aligned people might be an upside. Boy was that an under-statement! I find it makes a massive difference to my experience. But working alongside value-aligned people isn't much of a unique selling point on this forum.. so allow me to explain what’s special about AIM’s people and their values:

They take their principles seriously. This is the only reason our crazy salary policy works: At AIM, staff ask for the salary they need, and there’s no negotiation. The top of our range is more than double the bottom. “But everyone will ask for the top of the range!”, approximately everyone warned us before we rolled it out. It’s true that nothing stops them. We just ask staff to practise salary restraint (i.e. ask for what you need rather than the most you could get, since every dollar we don’t spend on ourselves can go towards helping beneficiaries instead), and then we trust them. So far, that trust has been well placed: Instead of uniformly shifting up, salaries have spread out according to need.

^It’s hard to convey warmth and authenticity through a blog.. this is the best I’ve got!

Some roles lean more senior:

1) Senior Research Manager (Animal Welfare): Lead our animal welfare research end to end, deciding which ideas become the next field-leading animal charities. This is hands-on research with a path into leading a growing team.

2) Senior Research Manager (Global Health & Development): As above. We’re looking both for people with more of a development economics background and classic global health background. for GHD.

^^ I just want to interrupt to emphasise how cool I think it is to be a researcher at AIM.. You recommend a set of charities that should exist, and within months, hot-shit co-founders will be dedicating their careers to building them. Very few research jobs have such a short, direct line from recommendation to action. Get hyped!

3) Special Projects Officer, Strategy: Work with our Chief Growth Officer and exec team to help us figure out what to build next and build it. Should we launch a fund? Should we incubate other incubators? How do we best support our existing charities to 10x their scale? This role is ideal for a sharp generalist, and consulting or strategy experience is a plus.

Others are a great way in, whether you’re early in your career or switching fields:

4) Marketing & Content Associate: Tell AIM’s story, and our charities’ stories, to the people who’ll become our next founders. You’ll own our ~20k mailing list, our new website, our social media and our founder application campaign. It's a creative, writing-led, hands-on role with a lot of variety.

5) Recruitment & Selection Associate: Help us sift a mountain of applications for the rare people who have what it takes to found a charity. Help us make our selection process more accurate over time. No recruitment experience needed: If you're curious about people and like fixing noisy rubrics, this is for you.

6) HR & Finance Associate: Own the people-and-money admin that keeps AIM running: contracts, payroll, onboarding, receiving grants and disbursing seed funding. This is for someone who likes to get the details right, and ideally likes automating them too. London preferred.

7) Visiting Research Fellow, Global Health: A five month fellowship embedded in our research team, for people with a background in global health, policy, epidemiology or medicine. You'll work on the same questions our research managers do, with more feedback and guidance. Past fellows have gone on to Prevail, Animal Charity Evaluators, Giving What We Can, Giving Green, Shrimp Welfare Project and AIM itself.

To pre-empt some misconceptions that might stop you from applying:

  • You don’t need to be deep in EA, though you do need to care about doing the most good, and be comfortable with numbers and uncertainty.
  • You don’t need to have done the job before. Some of our best hires hadn’t. Our first filter looks at your background and how you think about impact, and from there we assess mostly through test tasks and a paid work trial, so how well you do the work counts for more than what you’ve done before.
  • You don’t need to move to London. Most roles are remote-friendly. But if you’d like to, we’ll try to make it happen (we offer visa sponsorship and relocation support for most).

Not sure which role fits, or think you’d be great at something we haven’t listed? Fill in the expression of interest form anyway.

The process:

  • Taking the first step is trivially easy: Fill out our expression of interest form (5 mins). We’ll review applications on a rolling basis.
  • From there, each stage asks a bit more of you:
    • First a 30-minute role-specific application
    • Then a 2–3 hour test task
    • An interview and references, and
    • A paid work trial for the final one or two candidates. 

We only invite you to the next stage if we think you have a good chance of passing it.

Questions? Check out the job descriptions with more detail here or shoot us a note at hiring@ambitiousimpact.com,

Nothing for you? Many of our charities are scaling and hiring too: Probably Good maintains a list of their public job opportunities here.

To close

Did I rejoin Ambitious Impact at the wrong time? I don’t think so. But you could join at the wrong time, if you leave it too late: The people who join in the next year will determine AIM’s future. Our leverage and upside potential is reeaaally high. We need your talent to help us actually realize it.

  2. ^

Or for example, bans on cruel farming practices often have long phase-out periods to make them acceptable to industry, such that wins can take a decade to help their first animal.

item.title: Your work at [large AI safety ecosystem org] is not replaceable
item.description:
Published on October 15, 2026 5:48 PM GMT

When speaking to candidates who are considering working with us at 80,000 Hours, I often hear people worry about replaceability.

The familiar version of the worry is about whether the organisation will hire someone else in your place. If it will, then the difference you make by taking the job is only the difference between you and them.

There are a couple of well-known answers to that. The person hired in your place probably cares about the world too, and would go on to do something useful with their time instead (Ben Todd wrote about this in 2015). And in a hiring round, the top candidate is often a lot stronger than the next-best one (Rob Wiblin worked this through in 2019).

These days, I think it’s very common for organisations to do bar hiring rather than slot hiring: if we don’t hire you, we won’t hire anyone else.

If someone was considering joining as a podcast host or a writer, that would resolve the replaceability question: it’s clear that their addition to 80k is approximately equal to their podcast episodes or the pieces they write.

But for people in managerial or generalist roles, we often hear a different response to the replaceability worry, which goes something like this:

“80k is already doing pretty well. It’s big, stable, and it has a few committed senior people. If 80k doesn’t hire me, the staff who are already there will keep looking after whatever I would have done. That means I won’t have much impact there and I shouldn’t work there.”

I claim that this line of thinking is mistaken, because it doesn’t reason past the first-order counterfactual.

Of course, it’s literally true that a given responsibility could otherwise be done by someone else.

For example, you could join our People Operations team and run our September payroll. If you didn’t do it, then our Head of People Operations would run payroll. If she couldn’t do it then our Director of Operations would do it (or ask someone on her team to do it). And if she couldn’t do it then our Chief of Staff would do it (or ask someone else to do it).

It’s very unlikely that we don’t do our September payroll, so the first-order analysis shows that it’s entirely replaceable work.

Thinking through the second-order analysis (but skipping the third)[1], you’ll notice that our Head of People Operations might otherwise have done a deep dive into a tension in a management relationship and substantively improved how the two of them communicate, our Director of Operations might have reviewed the case for a solo Bay Area office and changed her mind on two aspects of it, and our Chief of Staff might otherwise have taken two meetings with speculative candidates to start new programmes.

Somewhere at the bottom of that chain is a piece of work which doesn’t get done: the deep dive, the office review, or the meetings with would-be programme founders.

It isn’t trivial to know what 80k will get done because someone is now running our payroll. But it is trivial to reason that something extra will be done. Similarly, if you accept an offer to join, it isn’t trivial for us to reason through what extra will be done because you came. But it is trivial to notice that, in expectation, we’ll be able to achieve more if we’re 56 people than if we’re 55.[2]

This means that if you are working at 80k, or in fact at any large organisation in the AI safety ecosystem[3], you’re really likely to be making a contribution which wouldn’t happen without you.

These might seem like straightforward points.

And they’ve been made before and more rigorously than I’m making them here.

But I do still run into the concern that working at a given organisation or in the field generally is replaceable.

So I’ve decided to emphasise what I’m saying here by whining about what it feels like to me when someone tells me that they don’t want to work at 80k because we don’t need them.

What follows is a description of the bottom of this chain at 80k: the things we think are worth doing, and aren’t doing.

Rant

We’ve been working on helping talented people tackle the world’s most pressing problems for 15 years, but the pressing problems still seem erm… Pretty bloody talent constrained.

Like, we are really really trying, and maybe we look like we’ve got our shit together, but in comparison to what our mission and the world are demanding from us, we just suck at what we do. And so we need your help.

I think that most of our existing programmes are markedly below the scale and impact which they could be operating at. I think our research and movement building strategy is further from the bleeding edge than it used to be. I think that we’ve probably lost ground relative to other efforts aimed at getting people into the field in the past couple of years, such that if we repeated the cross-sectional surveys we’d look worse than we previously did.

We totally missed the boat on fellowships. These turned into the ~best scaling movement building innovation of the past 5 years, but we never set one up — even though they’ve been on our radar since I joined in 2017.

We launched our AI career advisor in August 2026, a mere (checks notes) 2.75 years after we first prototyped the idea.

Marketing took us years to get off the ground and we’re still below where we’d like to be by a factor of somewhere between 3 and 30.[4]

I could go on.

I will go on.

We’ve repeatedly failed to spin up a strong headhunting service for the ecosystem. We had three false starts under different leads, using various approaches, and we’ve only recently begun scaling the approach we’re currently using. We’re well below our potential with the current (more scalable) version of headhunting — by at least a factor of 4.

We have wanted a YouTube channel like AI in Context for years (everyone was nagging us about it); we only managed to launch one last summer. And now that we have one, we wish we were publishing way more on it, being more ambitious with it, and running more channels. Also, we’re still not doing well at shortform video (TikTok etc.) — but surely there’s gotta be a viable strategy here…

The number of people we’ve given one-on-one advice to has flatlined since 2022.

We gave away half a million in talent development grants, then lost the ability to make grants when we spun out of Effective Ventures. We haven’t prioritised rebuilding it, as it would take some work (and probably also because we suck).

We didn’t spin out of Effective Ventures as early as we should have, our recruiting team started in January 2026 (after one false start), and we don’t have a US entity because we don’t have the capacity to set one up.

/rant

Overall, I just think it’s bloody contingent that we ended up being this level of good.

I think we’ve averaged something like 30% growth[5] a year across 80k.

Said like that, it sounds lovely and smooth, perhaps even overdetermined.

But I don’t think it’s been overdetermined, and I don’t think much of it has been a ‘top down’ decision based on reasoning through when we expect programmes to hit diminishing returns.

Instead, what we’ve been able to do seems extremely contingent on particular staff who managed to make particular contributions, and on particular staff who we failed to hire who didn’t make contributions.

It’s really easy for me to imagine an adjacent version of history where our overall growth rate was more like 50%, or where we shrank. Indeed, in some years, some programmes have more than doubled, in other years programmes have shrunk.

And it seems very possible to me that the returns on resources invested into 80k have increased about as often as they’ve decreased. I think it’s quite possible that our video programme is more cost effective than the rest of 80k: such that 80k saw increasing returns when we added it. And I’m fairly confident that our headhunting team is going through a period of increasing returns.

To summarise: I claim that, properly considered, your work at a given large AI safety ecosystem org is ~not replaceable.

I’ve given a few arguments for that, and I’ve done a lot of whining. I hope that you found at least one of those convincing.

    I think that it’s mostly fine to skip the third-order analysis, and just stop at the second.

    In a stable sector of the economy like healthcare, the number of doctors is set by things like demand and training places. So if you become a doctor, then over the long run someone else probably doesn’t. That’s the third-order analysis, and it’s where replaceability comes back in.

    You might want to review this 2014 piece on 80,000 Hours from the economist Rossa O’Keeffe-O’Donovan, on how to reason through how a given entrant affects aggregate supply into a sector over the long run.

    But AI safety is not a stable sector of the economy and in the short long run, we’re all dead.

    Instead, most of the organisations in AI safety are trying to absorb talent and funding at an extremely high rate, and the ecosystem isn’t in the kind of equilibrium which lends itself to O’Keeffe-O’Donovan’s reasoning above.

  2. ^

    This assumes the hire goes well. Some hires cost more in management and coordination than they add, at least at first, and that includes some people we’re very glad we hired. But we only make an offer when we expect it to work out, so in expectation the 56th person adds something.

  3. ^

    See footnote 1.

  4. ^

    I admit that 3–30 is quite a wide range to be unsure over. Especially for something which we’ve spent over 500 hours analysing. But, as discussed, we suck.

  5. ^

    By growth, I mean an output metric in quality adjusted careers affected. Like, impact as proxied by the a) number of careers we have affected by b) the amount we’ve affected those careers and c) how talented/motivated the people with those careers are. This is different to impact, but I didn’t want to say ‘increased our output’ because that just sounds like we’ve written more stuff or something. Incidentally, we’ve grown staff at roughly 25% per year.

item.title: We’re scaling and hiring
item.description:
Published on October 16, 2026 12:01 PM GMT

At Probably Good, our goal is to help people build careers that are good for them and for the world. We’re excited to share that, after exceeding expectations in our previous grant period, we just received a new grant from Coefficient Giving to significantly scale our work further. This comes at an important time for the effective careers ecosystem, which is working to help people navigate a rapidly changing job market as they tackle the world’s most pressing problems.

As a result, we’re currently hiring two people for our new Programs team. These roles center on 1:1 career advising: helping people think clearly about important career decisions and leave with practical next steps. Advisors who are interested can also spend up to half their time on headhunting (matching people with high-impact opportunities) or events (sharing our ideas with students and professional groups).

Some practical details:

  • Location: The roles are remote, with a strong preference for candidates who are available on weekdays for at least 3 hours between 12 PM and 5 PM GMT. 
  • Expected salary: $75,700 – $116,300 (US), £53,900 – £91,300 (UK), with adjustments for other locations based on cost of living.
  • Deadline: Applications close on 1 November, and we plan to make offers around mid-December.

There’s no single background we think is necessary for these roles. If you’re able to connect with people from lots of different backgrounds and thoughtfully steer them in the direction of having more impact with their careers, then we’d be excited to see you apply. And if you know someone who could be a fit for the roles, please forward them the job description.

As always, please let us know if you have any comments or questions!
